analysis.one_liner: Creates tax credits and grants to replace polluting fossil-fuel peaker power plants with renewable energy and battery storage near disadvantaged communities.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its May 2021 introduction, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there until the two-year Congress ended, with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Peaker plants are fossil-fuel power plants that fire up only when electricity demand spikes, such as during heat waves, and they tend to be located in low-income neighborhoods that already carry heavy pollution burdens. The PEAKER Act would have created a new 10% federal tax credit for renewable generation paired with battery storage, available only in communities near existing peaker plants, and set up a Department of Energy grant program of up to $1 billion a year through 2032 to help local governments, nonprofits, and community energy cooperatives build clean energy projects. It also would have required an annual public report on every peaker plant in the country, including how much pollution it emits and whether it sits in or near a disadvantaged community. The bill never advanced past its initial referral to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of disadvantaged communities that host or sit next to peaker plants, who breathe the nitrogen oxides, sulfur oxides, and fine particulate matter those plants emit on hot and cold days. Local governments, nonprofits, and community energy cooperatives in those neighborhoods would also gain access to grants covering up to 80% of project costs, and renewable energy and battery storage companies would gain a new tax credit and a dedicated pipeline of subsidized projects.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new 10% investment tax credit for renewable energy generation paired with battery storage, available only for projects placed in service in a disadvantaged community located in the same or an adjacent census tract as a peaker plant [S3].

Requires the storage portion to discharge electricity at the same times local peaker plants would run to meet peak demand, so the subsidized projects directly displace the fossil plants rather than just adding clean power to the grid [S3].

Establishes a Department of Energy grant program of up to $1 billion per year through fiscal 2032 for state and local governments, nonprofits, community-owned energy facilities, and energy cooperatives to build renewable and storage projects, implement community energy proposals, and fund community energy studies; community groups can get up to 80% of project costs covered, versus 60% for other applicants [S3].

Requires the Energy Department to produce an annual public report identifying every peaker plant, its pollution output, and whether it sits in or near a disadvantaged community, with public engagement required with residents of those communities [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the cost of the new tax credit and the grant program, which is authorized at up to $1 billion per year for fiscal years 2022 through 2032. Fossil-fuel peaker plant operators and their investors would eventually lose revenue as subsidized clean projects displace the need to run those plants during peak demand.

drawbacks.text: The bill would cost federal revenue: the new 10% tax credit reduces tax collections for every qualifying project, and the grant program is authorized at up to $1 billion per year for eleven fiscal years, so the total taxpayer cost over a decade could exceed $10 billion plus the tax expenditures [S2] [S3].

The tax credit and grants only apply to projects in the same or an adjacent census tract as a peaker plant, so most of the country gets nothing, and projects must discharge power exactly when local peaker plants would run, which requires grid-operator determinations that could slow deployment [S3].

Batteries and renewables replacing a peaker must match its ability to deliver power on the hottest and coldest days; if storage cannot fully match peaker output, some plants would keep running, so air-quality gains depend on how well the technology performs in practice [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The air-quality and health benefits are targeted at communities that carry a disproportionate pollution burden, which makes the spending efficient per dollar compared with broader clean-energy subsidies. The main cost is fiscal — a new tax credit plus up to $1 billion a year in grants for a decade — and the design has real frictions: eligibility tied to precise census-tract boundaries and grid-operator timing determinations could delay projects, and the credit alone may not be large enough to overcome the cost gap between batteries and cheap gas peakers in every market. On balance the design is purposeful rather than bloated, but its narrowness is also why it drew almost no co-sponsorship.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, and the Congress ended with it still parked in committee.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on May 11, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day [S1] [S5].
It attracted only 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, in a 100-member Senate [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of fossil-fuel peaker plants are better off: the plants that would have been replaced keep running and earning revenue, and no annual public accounting of their pollution was ever produced. The bill died so early and with so little support that no opponent needed to act against it.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PEAKER Act of 2021 on May 11, 2021 and shepherded its referral to the Senate Finance Committee [S1] [S3].

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; original cosponsor

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no other senator from either party joined [S4].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on May 11, 2021 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 20 months of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure party splits; the bill had only Democratic support (sponsor plus 2 cosponsors) and no Republican cosponsors ever signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill regulates peaker plants only indirectly — it reports on them and subsidizes replacements, but never caps their emissions, retires any plant, or imposes a fee on running them. Plants keep operating until a subsidized replacement is built in their specific census tract.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and battery storage developers
industries.note: A new 10% investment tax credit plus up to $1 billion a year in DOE grants creates a dedicated, location-specific customer base for solar, wind, geothermal, and battery storage developers in neighborhoods near peaker plants. The industry's gain and the public's health benefit run together here, but the subsidy also makes this industry the permanent channel for replacing peak power.

Utilities' fossil peaker units would face subsidized competition during peak hours, but utilities can also participate through partnerships with community entities applying for grants, so the bill opens a funding door for them as well.
